1:
The date is not incidental. Gill notes that the month answers to part of September and October, but Ellicott makes the day itself significant: the twenty-first of the seventh month was the last day of the Feast of Tabernacles, the festival of harvest thanksgiving, always marked by observances of a peculiarly joyous character, with sacrifices more numerous than on any other day of the year. On such a day both the scanty harvest and the small beginnings of the Lord's house would be brought into prominence, and despondency among those who remembered the temple of Solomon would be only natural. Henry dates it by the work instead, about a month after the builders began, and draws the rule that those hearty in the service of God receive fresh encouragements as their case calls for them, since if we set the wheels going God will oil them.

Who is addressed has widened. Keil and Delitzsch observes that the first appeal was made only to Zerubbabel and Joshua, whereas this comes also to the remnant of the nation, the whole congregation returned from exile. Henry notices that the encouragements are sent to the very people the previous chapter reproved, since those wounded by the convictions of the word are to be healed by its consolations. Gill attends to the wording: the old Greek wrongly renders the title as of the tribe of Judah, which neither distinguishes him nor answers a word expressing office, and some versions drop the particle rendered now, which is very emphatic, since the prophet was to speak that very day.

The discouragement itself is described at length by two of them. Henry says the damp on their joy was that they could not build such a temple as Solomon's; this had fetched tears when the dimensions were first laid, and still made the work go heavily, one remembering the gold with which the old house was overlaid, another the precious stones, another the magnificence of the porch, and all asking where these now were. He draws two lessons, that our proud hearts will scarcely let us be pleased with ourselves unless we do as well as others whose abilities far exceed ours, and that it is sometimes the fault of old people to discourage the present age by crying up the former, which should provoke emulation and not expose the present to contempt. Calvin traces the discouragement to a sharper source, having first answered how the comparison could be made days into the work, since the foundations had been laid long before and the building then interrupted for years. The faithful had learnt from Isaiah and Ezekiel, who even describes the form and dimensions of the house, that the temple built after the return would surpass the old one; so when they saw what they were building they were in danger of being wholly discouraged. He puts the temptation as a speech: what are you doing, you miserable men, you mean to build a temple to your God, and what sort of temple will it be, not the one all the prophets celebrated, for we are building a shed.

When the prophecy was spoken is settled from the same verse. Gill argues that it must have been under the earlier Darius, since those who take the other view must make these men nearly two hundred years old, far beyond the common length of life in that age, or else treat the words as a bare supposition, whereas they plainly imply that men then living had seen the first house in its glory. Clarke reckons more loosely that the foundation was laid some fifty-three years after the destruction of Solomon's temple and the prophecy uttered fifteen years later, so survivors might remain; Wesley puts the interval at near fourscore years. Ellicott renders the closing question as whether such a temple as this is not like nothing in their eyes.
4:
The threefold charge to be strong is taken as an answer to the discouragement just described. Gill paraphrases it as take heart, be of good courage, do not be dismayed; though the building may be contemptible in the eyes of some, go on with it manfully, since none should despise the day of small things and from these low beginnings great things will arise. To the governor in particular he applies the words as a charge to attend the work diligently, to continue presiding over it and encouraging the people, not letting the heart faint or the hands be slack, but acting the part of a man, of a good man, and of a governor. Keil and Delitzsch sets the promises out in order as they follow, that God is with them, that the word covenanted at the coming out of Egypt and his Spirit stand in the midst of them, and that they are therefore not to fear.

Clarke fixes on what the encouragement actually rests upon. The chief glory of the temple, he says, is not its splendid building but the divine presence, and as God covenanted to be with them when they came out of Egypt he will fulfil that covenant. He then turns the point on his own readers: what is the most splendid cathedral if God be not in it, influencing all by his presence and Spirit? and he adds that God will not be in it unless there is a messenger of the Lord there who delivers the Lord's message.

What the word in the next clause is divides two of them sharply. Ellicott renders it with the word rather than according to the word, and joins the clause to the close of the preceding verse, so that Jehovah is present with them and so is his promise made by solemn covenant in the days of old. Gill takes the same preposition in a different direction, reading it as with the Word in whom I covenanted, and understanding by that Christ, the essential Word, in whom all the promises are and the covenant of grace itself; on that reading the covenant was made with him from eternity and only more clearly manifested when the people came out of Egypt, and the promise here is that this same Word should be with the builders to counsel, assist, strengthen and protect them, as he had gone before their fathers in the pillar of cloud and of fire and had been the Angel of God's presence who saved and carried them all the days of old.

The spirit that remains among them is also read two ways. Ellicott prefers and my spirit to so my spirit, and takes it of the abiding presence of the Holy Spirit alongside the older promises of God's favour, adding that the evidence of that presence was the mission of inspired prophets such as Haggai and Zechariah; he allows that the Targum and the Rabbis are perhaps right in referring the words exclusively to the spirit of prophecy, and notes that the later Jews held the Holy Spirit to have left the church after the deaths of Zechariah and Malachi. Wesley keeps the sense broader and more practical, a spirit of strength and courage, of wisdom and understanding.
6:
The little while is measured variously. Calvin reports that most interpreters apply the smallness to time, a short duration after which God would make a change for the better, while others refer it to the subject itself, the temple not yet appearing in splendour; his concern is that the godly should not think God's power inefficient, but should let their minds pass from the present appearance to a restoration still distant. Ellicott calls the construction very difficult and renders it yet one season more, it is but a little while, the sense being that the interval before the predicted change is one uniform epoch and a brief one. He notes that the old Greek omits the clause about the little while and so can render I will yet shake once, meaning one single time only, which is impossible if the words are retained; and he lays down the principle that the original must be read without deference to the meaning it carries in a later argument. Wesley measures from the other end, that above five hundred years was still little compared with the space between the promise to Adam and the coming of Christ.

What the shaking is remains open. Clarke passes on the view of Newcome, that political and religious revolutions are both meant, and that the word once is clear if the evangelical age is intended, since many political revolutions succeeded one another but only one religious revolution. Wesley takes it as fulfilled metaphorically in the commotions among the Grecians and Romans and literally in prodigies and earthquakes. Ellicott declines the literal sense: the prophet speaks as the Hebrew poets do, painting divine interposition in colouring borrowed from the Exodus, and if the words are pressed their fulfilment must be looked for in the moral rather than the physical sphere, in the human heart rather than on the face of nature.

The desire of all nations is the crux. Clarke states the difficulty in the text itself: the reading is hard if a person is meant, since the noun for desire does not agree with a verb in the plural, and although some suppose the plural desirable things was the original reading, no manuscript supports it and the verb is nowhere found in the singular. He reports that it is generally understood of the valuable things the nations should bring, and that a bishop who laboured to vindicate the received translation is abandoned by the text.

Ellicott presses the point further and names the motive he thinks lies behind the other reading. He renders the clause the precious things of all the nations shall be brought as offerings, calls the received rendering grammatically impossible because the verb is plural, and says its retention in modern commentaries is mainly attributable to a natural unwillingness to give up a direct Messianic prophecy. Apart from the grammar he adds that the Messiah was not longed for by all nations, and that if he had been there would be no point in saying so here, whereas the prediction of Gentile offerings answers those who sorrowed over the mean appearance of the house and gives the verse about the silver and gold a meaning it otherwise lacks. Keil and Delitzsch reads it so as well, that God can fill the house with glory because the silver and gold the nations possess are his, and that by shaking the kingdoms he can induce them to present their treasures.

Gill and Wesley keep the older sense. Gill understands the passage of the Messiah and his times, resting on the apostle's application of it and on the ancient Jewish interpreters. Wesley names Christ as the most desirable, desired by all who knew their own misery and his sufficiency to save them, and contrasts the first house, whose glory of structure and rich ornaments was worldly, with the heavenly glory promised here from the presence of Christ.
8:
Why the silver and gold are mentioned at all is read two ways. Gill takes the clause as anticipating an objection drawn from the precious metals with which the first house was decorated and which would be wanting in the second: all the gold and silver in the world are the Lord's and at his disposal, so that whatever was bestowed on the former temple was only giving him his own; and were he so disposed he could command all the gold in the world into this house, but these are not the things he delights in. Ellicott rejects that turn expressly, calling it unnatural to suppose the words are said in the sense of having no need of silver or gold, and holding that what is meant is that the treasures of earth are at God's disposal and that he will incite the Gentiles to offer theirs in his temple; he adds that a rigid application of the prediction is impossible. Wesley reads it as simple assurance, that they need not doubt he will give enough to build the house.

How great the former glory was Gill sets out before comparing. He lists the treasure David had laid up, the number of workmen, the stateliness of a fabric whose model was drawn by the Lord himself, the vessels, and above all the glory of the Lord which filled it; a glory must be very great indeed, he says, that exceeds this. He then reports what the Jews themselves own was wanting in the second house, the ark, the Urim and Thummim, the fire from heaven, the Shechinah and the Holy Ghost, which makes the promise harder rather than easier to account for.

Where the greater glory lay is answered carefully by Clarke. He denies that it can consist in the personal appearance of Christ in that house, or rather in the house built by Herod, since though we allow that Christ is equal with God we do not grant that he is greater, and the first temple had been the dwelling-place of God, who manifested his glory there between the cherubim for four hundred years. The glory of the latter house was greater, he says, because under it the grand scheme of human salvation was exhibited and the redemption price was paid down for a lost world; and since the promise probably applies to the Christian church, the real house of God, its glory was certainly greater than any the Jews ever possessed.

Ellicott takes the wording rather than the theology. He prefers to render it the latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former, and observes that the new sanctuary is regarded as identical with the one reared by Solomon, so that it would have a claim to celebrity unrivalled even in the palmiest days of old. He also marks the interval that follows, since between this utterance and the next comes the exhortation to repentance delivered by Zechariah in the eighth month. Keil and Delitzsch dates the next word exactly, three months after the congregation resumed the building and about two months after the second prophecy, by which time the despondency that had seized the people had been dispelled and the work was going vigorously forward.

The peace at the end of the promise is taken in more than one sense. Clarke notes that the word means a peace-offering as well as peace itself, and applies it to Christ, called the Prince of peace, through whom peace is proclaimed between God and man and established in the disconsolate soul, adding that it was at this temple that such peace was first promulgated. Wesley keeps to the thing rather than the offering, a spiritual, internal and heavenly peace, and reads the place itself as a type.
10:
Gill places the new date in the month answering to part of November and December, two months after the previous message and three months from the day the people began work on the house. Henry observes that the priests preached constantly while the prophets preached occasionally, both being good and needful, since we have need to be taught our duty in season and out of season.

Why a prophet is told to consult the priests is Henry's chief interest. Their lips should keep this knowledge, he says, and the people should enquire the law at their mouth, so that Haggai himself, though a prophet, must ask them: his own business was to expound providences and give directions about particular duties, and he would not take the priests' work out of their hands. From this he draws the rule that God gives his ministers diversities of gifts and calls them to diversities of services, so that the prophet cannot say to the priest, I have no need of thee. He adds that Haggai may have been ordered to consult them so that out of their own mouths he might judge them, and convict them of something worse than ceremonial pollution.

The two questions and their answers are stated plainly. Clarke sets them side by side, that holiness carried in the skirt of a garment does not pass to what the skirt touches, to which the priests answered no, and that uncleanness from a dead body does, to which they answered yes. Gill explains that the holy flesh is that of creatures offered in sacrifice, part of which belonged to the priests, who carried it in the skirts of their garments; Wesley adds that it was made holy by the altar. Ellicott states the principle behind the pair: the sacrifice hallowed the person who touched it, but not anything he afterwards touched, whereas one defiled by contact with a dead body conveyed defilement even to the tabernacle. So the guilt incurred in neglecting the temple had tainted the labour of their hands and caused the famine, while whatever merit they claimed for restoring the altar-worship was cancelled by the neglect of an equally important duty; and this last point, he notes, is not brought out but left for the hearers to supply. Keil and Delitzsch gives the aim more briefly, to impress on the people that the failure of the crops was a punishment brought on by their own sin.

Calvin thinks every one of these readings falls short. He says that although interpreters seem to perceive the prophet's meaning, no one really expresses it, and that what they adduce is jejune and frigid, since they refer the whole to the point that sacrifices were unacceptable before the building began and acceptable afterwards. That is part of it, he grants, but not the whole. His own view is that the prophet, having exhorted them to build, now exhorts them to build from a pure motive, and not to suppose they had done everything once the temple looked well. The command to build had been given so that God might be worshipped purely; he never cared for external ceremonies, nor was he delighted with a building as men are with their houses, and worship is corrupted whenever confined to external things, since God is thereby transformed into a nature not his own. As he is a Spirit, Calvin says, he must be spiritually worshipped, and whoever obtrudes outward pomp to pacify him trifles childishly.

He also grades their conduct in three stages: neglecting the building showed their impiety; undertaking it strenuously was a proof of piety; but thinking God required nothing beyond a splendid temple was manifest superstition. Henry reaches a similar caution, that a work good in its matter must also be done in a right manner or it will not be accepted.
13:
The second question turns the rule the other way. Ellicott notes that defilement from a dead body was one of the deepest known to the law, and Wesley states the logic of the pair: though a mediate touch of what is holy will not make holy, a mediate touch of what is polluted will defile. Clarke draws the application: as an unclean man communicates his uncleanness to everything he touches, so were they unclean, and whatever they had done was polluted, their neglect of the temple having made them unclean as if they had touched a corpse. Wesley presses the point on the worship itself, that polluted people polluted the ordinances, the outward performing of legal duties leaving them as unholy as before, so the soul must first be purified before a pure offering can be made. Ellicott adds that what they offer there probably means on yon altar, though the phrase is singular.

Which way the reckoning runs is disputed. Ellicott says plainly that upward here means backward, the reference being to the recent resumption of the building rather than to the foundations laid fifteen years before; Gill and Wesley read it the same way. Calvin argues the opposite. He observes that the word is applied to time in only two other places, where it clearly means forward, and carries the same sense when applied to age and to place; if that meaning is kept, this verse and its repetition further down open a single long sentence not completed until the end of the passage, everything between standing as parenthesis. He also prefers to render the idiom of setting the heart as mark rather than consider, and reports three manuscripts reading your rather than their below.

Calvin explains why the argument is pitched so low. The prophet speaks in a homely manner to earthly men addicted to their appetites; had they grown wiser he might have addressed them differently, following the rule that wisdom is spoken among the perfect, but since their thoughts were fixed on meat and drink he tells them what they could comprehend, that God was angry and the proofs of his curse evident in a soil that gave no fruit. In this Calvin finds an indirect reproach of their insensibility, since the prophet does not direct their thoughts to heaven or announce deep mysteries but speaks only of food and daily support, so that to overlook such marks of wrath was an intolerable stupidity.

The failed harvests are reckoned exactly. Clarke states them as a heap of corn that should have produced twenty measures producing ten, and grapes that would have yielded fifty yielding twenty, and this ever since the first stone was laid. Ellicott renders the opening as from the time when things were so, notes that the measure for the heap is not specified, and observes that the word for the vessel elsewhere means a winepress but here is apparently the bucket used to draw the wine up. Gill puts the period at fifteen or sixteen years, and Wesley sums it up as men disappointed half in half.

The plagues named are traced to older lists. Ellicott calls the clause a reminiscence of Amos, that God had smitten them with blasting and mildew and yet they had not returned to him, and points out that both are diseases of corn enumerated by Moses among the curses on disobedience, while the hail is added by Haggai, perhaps as particularly destructive to the vines. Gill explains the first as burning winds and blights on the east wind, and says they are named to show that the disappointment came from the Lord and for their sins. Keil and Delitzsch marks the turn that follows, that after appealing to them to lay to heart the time the blessing had been withheld, the prophet calls them to fix their eyes on the time beginning that day.
18:
The renewed call to consider is read as marking a change of direction. Gill notes that the word may be rendered forward as well as upward, of time to come, as one old version has it; Wesley takes it from the day they began to build on the old foundation; and Clarke gives the sense as a change in God's own conduct, that from the day they began heartily to rebuild the temple and restore his worship he would bless them, so that whatever they sowed or planted should be blessed and the land be fruitful.

Ellicott finds the received rendering of the second half impossible. Better, he says, even to the day rather than even from the day, since as it stands the passage is quite unintelligible: in no sense can the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month coincide with the day the foundation of the temple was laid, that foundation having been laid fifteen years earlier, in the second month of the second year of Cyrus. The building had then gone on intermittently until within two years of this message, had been entirely suspended, and had only been taken actively in hand after the prophet's address in the sixth month of the current year. On his rendering the point is that, in order to set the promised blessings in strong contrast to the distress just described, the prophet repeats his injunction but with a longer range of retrospect, the whole period back to the founding under Cyrus having been more or less one of distress on account of the unfaithfulness of the people, since every effort made in that interval to complete the work was spasmodic and feeble. He grants that his own rendering, though allowable, rests on a construction that is certainly rare.

What state the harvest was actually in divides the readers three ways. Wesley takes the question as answered yes, that the seed for the next harvest was still in the barns, so that no sign yet appeared what vintage there would be, what store of wine and oil and figs and pomegranates, and yet the promise of a large produce is given. Gill reports that some do answer in the affirmative, since the ninth month answers to part of November, but prefers the negative, that the seed was by then just sown, so that no conjecture could be made whether the harvest would be good or bad; and he supports this by noting that the ninth month, and indeed only the first half of it, was the last season for sowing, which makes the promise all the more remarkable for being given so long beforehand. Ellicott reads the clause as a statement of want rather than of timing: there is no grain as yet in the barn, the harvest having been blighted in the last season, and the word rendered seed does not mean grain for sowing but grain for provision. On his account the fruit harvest was as defective as the cereals, having been cut off by the hail already mentioned, so that the prospect was one of the deepest gloom; but human helplessness, he says, is God's opportunity, and it is at that crisis that the promise to bless is given.

Keil and Delitzsch marks what follows on the same day. The Lord had just promised the return of the blessings of nature, and now the prophet receives a second revelation, promising the community the preservation and care of the house of David, represented for the time by Zerubbabel, in the midst of the storms about to burst upon the power of the world.
20:
The last word comes the same day, and to one man. Gill and Clarke note that it was a second communication on the same date, and Henry describes the change of audience: after a sermon to the people there follows one to the magistrate. Henry then contrasts their two anxieties. The people are in care about their corn-fields and vineyards, and have just been assured these will prosper; but the governor is concerned about the neighbouring nations and the revolutions of their governments, about what will become of a few feeble Jews in such convulsions, and how so poor a prince is to keep his ground. To him God sends word that it shall be well with him, and that is to make him easy.

The shaking is announced a second time and read as before. Henry tells him to expect shaking times, since the world is like the sea, always in motion but sometimes in a special manner turbulent; but if the earth is shaken, he adds, it is to shake the wicked out of it, and in the apocalyptic visions earthquakes bode no ill to the church. However powerful the kingdoms, their strength shall be destroyed by the sword of brother against brother.

Calvin rejects one reading of the shaking. Some take it of a continued act, so that although it belongs to God to shake heaven and earth and subvert kingdoms, he will nevertheless make firm the sacred kingdom he has raised among his people; Calvin calls that very frigid. He holds instead that God intimates some memorable work in contemplation, which when done would make heaven and earth tremble, and that the prophet is leading the Jews to hope for a redemption whose fullness was then hidden, since who could have expected such a renovation of the world as the coming of Christ effected? Exposed to the wrongs of all men and with no kingdom and no power, they had thought themselves as it were deceived. He also distinguishes this promise from the last, which concerned corn and wine, while this is an undertaking to be an eternal Father to the people.

Which upheaval is meant has been answered several ways. Clarke reports that Calmet supposed the invasion of Cambyses and his death, objects that this happened three years before the work on the temple began and could hardly interest the governor now, and notes that Calmet answered by rendering the verbs in the past tense, so the event was recalled to fix his confidence in God. He gives the alternatives of Newcome, the calamity undergone by Babylon under Darius, the Macedonian conquests, or the wars of Alexander's successors, and adds that others understand it of the Romans. Gill takes the throne of kingdoms as the Persian monarchy, destroyed under its last king by Alexander in three pitched battles, and insists the thing was of the Lord; he corrects a reckoning that put its fall thirty-four years after the building of the temple, since it lasted longer.

The signet at the close is taken as a figure of value. Clarke reads it as exaltation to high dignity and trust, of which the seal was the sign in those days, so that the man addressed should be under God's peculiar care; Ellicott notes only that the figure is applied to one on whom confidence and affection are bestowed. Gill argues from the opening words that the promise cannot be understood literally of the governor, since the day meant is the day when all these kingdoms are destroyed, and he did not live to see it. Wesley takes the same view and completes it, making him a type of the most beloved servant of God: as a signet is highly valued and carefully kept, so the Messiah is advanced, loved and inviolably preserved, all power being given to him and all the promises in him yea and amen.
